full_text: Ct. Cases No. 8521/2019 Kailash Chand vs . Deevansh Bhatia Page No. 1 Of 15 on 30 July, 2026 IN THE COURT OF SHRI TANMAY BATHAM, JUDICIAL MAGISTRATE FIRST CLASS, NI ACT - 03, TIS HAZARI DISTRICT COURTS (WEST), DELHI JUDGMENT SH. KAILASH CHAND S/o Sh. Jai Chand R/o: D-26, Hari Nagar, New Delhi - 110064 ... COMPLAINANT VERSUS SH. DEEVANSH BHATIA S/o Sh. Gunjan Bhatia R/o: B-7, Top Floor, Kiran Garden, Uttam Nagar, New Delhi - 110059 ... ACCUSED Ct. Cases No. 8521/2019 Offence complained of Dishonour of Cheque u/s 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 Plea of Guilt Not Guilty Final Order Conviction Date of Pronouncement 30.07.2026 • Argued by: Mr. Anil Kumar Singh, Ld. Counsel for the Complainant. Mr. Gaurav Garg, Ld. Counsel for the Accused. FACTUAL MATRIX 1. The present complaint is filed by the complainant Mr. Kailash Chand (hereinafter referred to as the "Complainant") against the accused Mr. Deevansh Bhatia (hereinafter referred to as the "Accused") under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (hereinafter referred to as " NI Act "). The substance of allegations of the complainant is that he is having cordial terms TANMAY Digitally signed by TANMAY BATHAM BATHAM Date: 2026.07.30 15:39:26 +0530 Ct. Cases No. 8521/2019 Kailash Chand vs. Deevansh Bhatia Page No. 1 of 15 with the accused and owing to the same relationship, the accused approached him to take a loan of Rs. 3,80,000/- in the end January, 2017 for the purpose of investment in his business. That on the assurances of accused of returning the money within six months, the complainant advanced a loan of Rs. 3,80,000/- to the accused, in cash, which was duly received by the accused in presence of witnesses and the accused also executed and Undertaking/Promissory Note dated 01.02.2017 (Ex. CW1/1). That the accused had assured that in case he fails to repay the said loan within six months, then the complainant will be entitled to take legal actions and he will pay interest @ 18% per annum. 2. That upon passage of six months and after several requests by the complainant, the accused, in discharge of the aforesaid liability, issued a post dated cheque (hereinafter referred to as the "Cheque in question") bearing the following particulars: • Cheque bearing no. 052563 and dated 23.08.2019; for a quoted amount of Rs. 3,80,000/-, drawn on ICICI Bank, Tilak Nagar Branch, New Delhi. That, the cheque in question (Ex. CW1/2) was presented in the bank of the complainant and was returned back unpaid vide return memo (Ex. CW1/3) dated 27.08.2019 with the remark of "Funds Insufficient". That the complainant then issued a legal demand notice (Ex. CW1/4), dated 24.09.2019, dispatched through speed-post receipt (Ex. CW1/5) and purportedly delivered on the accused, as being shown in the copy of tracking report (Ex. CW1/6). That the accused has failed to reply to the legal demand notice or to make the payment of the cheque amount within stipulated time; hence the present complaint has been filed. NOTICE U/S 251 CRPC 3. On finding a prima facie case against the accused, he was summoned to TANMAY Digitally signed by TANMAY BATHAM BATHAM Date: 2026.07.30 15:24:40 +0530 Ct. Cases No. 8521/2019 Kailash Chand vs. Deevansh Bhatia Page No. 2 of 15 face trial and upon his appearance, a notice of accusation under Section 251 , Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (hereinafter referred to as " Cr.P.C ") was served on him. In reply to the notice of accusation, the accused pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. Therein, he admitted his signatures on the cheque in question, but denied filling the particulars on it. He also denied receiving the legal demand notice. He stated that his nephew Akash Gera wanted to get a mobile phone financed from one financer and he gave the cheque in question to his nephew. He stated that he does not know the complainant and has no transactions with him. He further stated that he does not know how the complainant came into possession of the cheque in question. He stated that the complainant has filed a false case after misusing his cheque. COMPLAINANT'S EVIDENCE 4. Thereafter, upon application of accused under Section 145 (2) NI Act seeking permission to cross-examine the complainant, the same was allowed. During the trial, in the Complainant's Evidence (hereinafter referred to as "CE"), the complainant has led both oral and documentary evidence against the accused to prove his case beyond reasonable doubt. The Complainant himself stepped in the witness box as CW-1 and tendered his evidence by way of affidavit which is Ex. CW1/A. He further relied upon the following documents: Srl. No. Title of Document Exhibited As 1 Undertaking / Promissory Note dated 01.02.2017 Ex. CW1/1 2 Cheque in Question bearing no. 052563 Ex. CW1/2 3 Cheque Returning Memo Ex. CW1/3 4 Legal Demand Notice Ex. CW1/4 5 Postal Receipts Ex. CW1/5 6 Tracking Report Ex. CW1/6 7 Affidavit of Complainant dated 23.12.2019 Ex. CW1/7 Digitally signed TANMAY by TANMAY BATHAM BATHAM Date: 2026.07.30 15:30:13 +0530 Ct. Cases No. 8521/2019 Kailash Chand vs. Deevansh Bhatia Page No. 3 of 15 The Complainant was duly cross examined by ld. Counsel for accused and all the exculpatory suggestions put to him were duly denied by him. STATEMENT OF ACCUSED 5. Thereafter, before the start of defence evidence, in order to allow the accused to personally explain the incriminating circumstances appearing in evidence against him, the statement of the accused was recorded without oath under Section 313 Cr.P.C. In reply, the accused denied taking any amount from the complainant or signing the Promissory Note (Ex. CW1/1). He denied receiving the legal demand notice and stated that the address mentioned therein is incorrect. He stated that his nephew Akash Gera has issued his blank signed cheques alongwith other documents, at the time of getting his mobile financed from someone in Hari Nagar. He denied owing any amount to the complainant. DEFENCE EVIDENCE 6. Thereafter, the accused was given an opportunity to led his defence evidence (hereinafter referred to as "DE"), upon which he stepped into the witness box as DW-1 and exhibited his Bank Account Statement for the period 09.11.2015 to 26.11.2019 as Ex. DW1/1, to show that his bank account has been inactive for the said period. FINAL ARGUMENTS 7. The final arguments were heard in the matter. I have heard the ld. counsels appearing for the parties and I have given my thoughtful consideration to the material appearing on record. 8. Following arguments have been advanced by the ld. counsel for the complainant: a) That all the ingredients of the offence are fulfilled in the present case. That the admission of the accused regarding his signatures, when seen in Digitally signed by TANMAY TANMAY BATHAM BATHAM 15:30:21 Date: 2026.07.30 +0530 Ct. Cases No. 8521/2019 Kailash Chand vs. Deevansh Bhatia Page No. 4 of 15 light of Section 118 (a) and Section 139 of the NI Act, shifts the onus upon the accused to prove the contrary that the cheque was not given in discharge of any liability; and that the accused has not been able to raise any probable defence regarding the same. b) That the Promissory Note (Ex. CW1/1), shows the admission of the liability of the accused and his denial of signature on the same will be of no value as he has lost his credibility as a witness when he denied his signatures on his own Bail Bonds. c) That the accused has dropped his best defence witness Akash Gera despite him being his own nephew, thereby showing the farce behind his defence. d) That the mobile phone referred by the accused in his cross-examination was launched in the year 2025 itself and hence the defence of the accused is false and fabricated. e) That the accused has not taken any other criminal action against the complainant for misuse of his cheque, thereby tacitly admitting his liability. As such, it is prayed that the accused be punished for the said offence. 9. Per contra, ld. counsel for the accused has argued on the following grounds: a) That the complainant has failed to establish his case beyond reasonable doubt. It is argued that the complainant has not brought on record any proof regarding the alleged friendly loan or friendly terms between the him and the accused. b) That the complainant has not led any expert evidence despite the accused denying his signatures on the Promissory Note (Ex. CW1/1). c) That the legal demand notice has not been served on the accused as he had left the said address in 2012. d) That as per the judgment of Hon'ble Hight Court of Jharkhand in Md. Digitally signed by TANMAY TANMAY BATHAM BATHAM 15:30:30 Date: 2026.07.30 +0530 Ct. Cases No. 8521/2019 Kailash Chand vs. Deevansh Bhatia Page No. 5 of 15 Masudul Haque Ansari @ M. H. Ansari vs. The State of Jharkhand (Acquittal Appeal No. 10 of 2012), a friendly loan without any consideration cannot be legally enforced. As such, it is prayed that the accused be acquitted. INGREDIENTS OF THE OFFENCE AND DISCUSSION 10. At the very outset, it would be appropriate to examine the legal requirements that both parties must meet before delving into the peculiar facts of the present case. The complainant must satisfy the following five essential components to make out the offence under section 138 NI Act: - First Ingredient: The cheque was drawn by a person on an account maintained by him for payment of money and the same is presented for payment within a period of 3 months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity; Second Ingredient: The cheque was drawn by the drawer for discharge of any legally enforceable debt or other liability; Third Ingredient: The cheque was returned unpaid by the bank due to either insufficiency of funds in the account to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account on an agreement made with that bank; Fourth Ingredient: A demand of the said amount has been made by the payee or holder in due course of the cheque by a notice in writing given to the drawer within thirty days of the receipt of information of the dishonour of cheque from the bank; Fifth Ingredient: The drawer fails to make payment of the said amount of money within fifteen days from the date of receipt of notice. 11. The accused can only be held guilty of the offence under Section 138 NI Act if all of the above-mentioned ingredients are proved by the complainant co- extensively. Additionally, the conditions stipulated under Section 142 NI Act have to be fulfilled. First and Third Ingredient 12. The proof of first and third ingredient is not disputed. The complainant has proved the original cheque, Ex. CW1/2, which the accused has not disputed as being drawn on his account. It is not disputed that the cheque in question was presented within the validity period. The cheque in question was returned unpaid TANMAY Digitally signed by TANMAY BATHAM BATHAM 15:30:38 Date: 2026.07.30 +0530 Ct. Cases No. 8521/2019 Kailash Chand vs. Deevansh Bhatia Page No. 6 of 15 vide return memo, Ex. CW1/3 due to the reason i.e., "Funds Insufficient". As such, on the basis of the above, the first and third ingredient of the offence under Section 138 NI Act stands proved. Fourth And Fifth Ingredient 13. With regard to the fourth ingredient, the complainant has proved on record the legal demand notice Ex. CW1/4 and effective dispatch of same through postal receipt Ex. CW1/5 and copy of tracking report Ex. CW1/6, which shows the legal demand notice to be duly served on the accused. The accused in his statement of admission and denial u/s 294 Cr.P.C, has denied receiving the legal demand notice. In his cross-examination, the accused has stated that he has left the address mentioned in the legal demand notice in the year 2012. The ld. counsel for the accused has argued that since the legal demand notice has not been sent on the correct address of the accused, the essentials of the offence u/s 138 of NI Act are not met. 14. The ld. counsel for the complainant has argued that the accused has slyly and wrongly denied his address on the legal demand notice. He submits that the complainant has duly averred in his evidence affidavit (Ex. CW1/A) that the legal demand notice has been sent on the correct address of the accused. He argues that when Bailable Warrants were issued against the accused on 30.11.2022, they were received back duly executed on 18.01.2023 wherein the accused had himself filled the same address as the one mentioned in the legal demand notice; and the accused had duly appeared after execution on the said address. He further argues that the accused has, otherwise also, not brought on record any evidence or any witness to show that he has left his address in 2012, due to which the legal demand notice has not been served on him. 15. A fair consideration of facts, in fact, reflects that the Bailable Warrants Digitally signed TANMAY by TANMAY BATHAM BATHAM Date: 2026.07.30 15:30:45 +0530 Ct. Cases No. 8521/2019 Kailash Chand vs. Deevansh Bhatia Page No. 7 of 15 were executed on the same address as the one mentioned in the legal demand notice; and thereby the blatant denial of the accused regarding his address on the legal demand notice shows his lack of bona fide and shakes his credibility as a witness. Nevertheless, it could be concluded that the legal demand notice was sent on the last known address of the accused. 16. It is a settled position that, once it has been established that the legal demand notice by the complainant was sent on the last known address of the accused, a presumption in the light of the Section 27 of the General Clauses Act and Section 114 of the Evidence Act will come into play and it could be reasonably presumed that the legal demand notice was served on the accused in usual course of business. Further, in CC Alavi Haji Vs. Palapetty Muhammed & Anr. (Crl . Appeal No. 767 of 2007), the Hon'ble Apex Court has held that: "Any drawer who claims that he did not receive the notice sent by post, can, within 15 days of receipt of summons from the court in respect of the complaint under section 138 of the Act, make payment of the cheque amount and submit to the court that he had made payment within 15 days of receipt of summons (by receiving a copy of complaint with the summons) and therefore, the complaint is liable to be rejected. A person who does not pay within 15 days of receipt of the summons from the court along with the copy of the complaint under Section 138 of the Act, cannot obviously contend that there was no proper service of notice as required under section 138 , by ignoring statutory presumption to the contrary under section 27 of the General Clauses Act and Section 114 of the Evidence Act". Therefore, the statement of the accused that the address on the legal demand notice is incorrect, will not hold much strength in the light of the discussion regarding his address. Hence, the complainant can be said to have sufficiently discharged the requirement of sending the legal demand notice at the last known address of the accused. Accordingly, the fourth ingredient stands proved. 17. The fact that the payment was not made within 15 days of the receipt of the legal notice is also not disputed. Therefore, the fifth ingredient of the offence also stands proved. Second Ingredient TANMAY Digitally signed by TANMAY BATHAM BATHAM Date: 2026.07.30 15:30:54 +0530 Ct. Cases No. 8521/2019 Kailash Chand vs. Deevansh Bhatia Page No. 8 of 15 18. Now, it remains to be ascertained if the second ingredient is proved or not. As far as the proof of second ingredient is concerned, it has to be proved that the cheque in question was drawn by the drawer for discharging a legally enforceable debt. In the present case, the signature of the accused on the cheque in question is not denied. In the plea of defence u/s 251 Cr.P.C, and in the statement u/s 313 Cr.P.C., the accused has admitted being a signatory to the cheque in question. Under the NI Act , once the accused admits his signatures on the cheque, certain presumptions are drawn, which result in shifting of onus. Section 118(a) of the NI Act lays down the presumption that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration. The second presumption is contained under Section 139 of NI Act which casts a reverse onus upon the accused. The provision lays down the presumption that the holder of the cheque received it for the discharge, in whole or part, of any debt or other liability. 19. It has been held by a three-judge bench of the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Rangappa vs. Sri Mohan (2010) 11 SCC 441 that the presumption contemplated under Section 139 of NI Act includes the presumption of existence of a legally enforceable debt. The principles pertaining to the presumptions and the onus of proof were recently summarised by the Hon'ble Apex Court in Basalingappa vs. Mudibasappa (2019) 5 SCC 418, whereby it has been held that as under: 25. We having noticed the ratio laid down by this Court in the above cases on Section 118(a) and 139 , we now summarise the principles enumerated by this Court in the following manner: 25.1. Once the execution of cheque is admitted Section 139 of the Act mandates a presumption that the cheque was for the discharge of any debt or other liability. 25.2. The presumption under Section 139 is a rebuttable presumption and the onus is on the accused to raise probable defence and the standard of proof for rebutting the presumption is that of preponderance of probabilities. 25.3. To rebut the presumption, it is open for the accused to rely on evidence led by him or the accused can also rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise a probable defence. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by the parties but also by reference to the circumstances upon which they rely. TANMAY Digitally signed by TANMAY BATHAM BATHAM Date: 2026.07.30 15:31:01 +0530 Ct. Cases No. 8521/2019 Kailash Chand vs. Deevansh Bhatia Page No. 9 of 15 25.4. That it is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box in support of his defence. Section 139 imposed an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden. In view of the above principles, a reverse onus is cast on the accused who has to establish a probable defence on the standard of preponderance of probabilities to prove that there was no legally enforceable debt or other liability. The arguments raised on behalf of the accused have been considered in totality and have been contrasted with his plea of defence taken u/s 251 Cr.P.C., his statement u/s 313 Cr.P.C. and the evidence brought on record. The contentions raised by the accused are being discussed below. CONTENTIONS OF THE ACCUSED TO REBUT THE PRESUMPTION (A) That the Complainant has not been able to establish that he had friendly terms with the Accused: 20. The ld. counsel for the accused has argued that the reading of the cross- examination of the CW-1 shows that there were no friendly terms between the parties. He argues that the complainant is a 47 year old man, having a big age gap with the accused, which makes it unlikely that they are friends to each other. A question was asked to the complainant if he had gone to any Movies or Restaurant with the accused ever, to which he replied with a No. On the basis of this and similar line of questioning, the ld. counsel for the accused has argued that no friendly terms have been proved between the parties and the case of the complainant has failed to stand on its own legs, hence the complaint is liable to be dismissed. 21. At this stage, it is important to be reminded that the concept of "friendly loan" under the NI Act is not tantamount to the test of who knows more about the other. The concept of friendly loan is a euphemism for the loans that are given in an informal structure in the society, and its existence cannot be disregarded merely because the accused and the complainant have not gone on Digitally signed TANMAY by TANMAY BATHAM BATHAM Date: 2026.07.30 15:31:07 +0530 Ct. Cases No. 8521/2019 Kailash Chand vs. Deevansh Bhatia Page No. 10 of 15 outings together. More importantly, it is also not the case that to nullify the claim of friendly loan, the accused has himself brought forth an alternate probable explanation, thereby rebutting the presumption under Section 139 r/w Section 118 (a) of the NI Act. The accused has taken a defence that the signed documents and the blank signed cheque in question was given to his nephew Akash Gera, who had used it for financing his mobile phone of the make and model - Samsung A26. The accused has not produced any bills of the said mobile to substantiate his version. The accused has even failed to call his nephew Akash Gera in the witness box, who would've proved his version by giving a direct evidence in his favour; thereby raising serious doubts on his version. Reliance can be placed in this regard in the observations of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in Hiten P. Dalal vs Bratindranath Banerjee [2001 (6) SCC 16] , wherein the following has been held in the para 24: "The words 'unless the contrary is proved' which occur in this provision make it clear that the presumption has to be rebutted by 'proof' and not by a bare explanation which is merely plausible." Hence, it becomes clear that merely presenting alternate version regarding the cheque being given to his nephew for financing go mobile, without any proof thereof, would not rebut the presumption against the accused. The accused has to prove what is being asserted by him in his defence, which has not been done in the present case, at any rate. 22. Interestingly, the accused was asked to clarify on the point that when the said make and model - Samsung A26 was itself launched in the year 2025, how could the nephew of the accused had bought it in the year 2017. The accused simply replied that he doesn't know when the said mobile was launched in the market. The line of questioning of the ld. counsel for the complainant has revealed that the defence taken by the accused has not found any firm ground to stand upon. The infirmity in the defence on the accused raises questions on his credibility as a witness, for the second time in this assessment. When the accused TANMAY Digitally signed by TANMAY BATHAM BATHAM Date: 2026.07.30 15:31:13 +0530 Ct. Cases No. 8521/2019 Kailash Chand vs. Deevansh Bhatia Page No. 11 of 15 has himself failed to bring forth any alternate and probable version of the facts, he cannot be allowed to evade his liability by simply denying having any friendly terms with the complainant, especially when his credibility as a witness has been shaken. 23. Even in arguendo, if the version of the accused is to be taken on the face value, it would show that he had admitted that he had voluntarily given the cheque in question to his nephew with the knowledge that the same is going to be used towards the mobile financing. Nowhere throughout the trial, the accused has alleged any mala fide in the manner in which Akash Gera has acquired the cheque in question from the accused. When the cheque in question was given by the accused to Akash Gera with the knowledge that it is being asked for the purpose of financing; and when the same cheque has been transferred ahead to some third person for that purpose, who may or may not be the complainant, the accused loses the ground to call it a misuse. In the bare reading of the Section 9 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, it would show that the said shopkeeper would be called "Holder in due course". Hence, even the best defence of the accused has not landed well in favour of the accused. Accordingly, the argument of the ld. counsel for the accused that the complaint is liable to be dismissed because the complainant has not been able to prove friendly terms with the accused, is rejected. (B) That the Complainant has not been able to produce any proof of the alleged loan in question: 24. The complainant has produced the Promissory Note (Ex. CW1/1), which purportedly records the accused's acknowledgement of the loan in question. The accused has denied singing the said Promissory note. It is argued by the ld. counsel for the accused that once the accused has denied his signatures on the Promissory Note (Ex. CW1/1), the complainant should have led evidence of an expert witness to establish the genuineness of the said Promissory Note. TANMAY Digitally signed by TANMAY BATHAM BATHAM Date: 2026.07.30 15:31:21 +0530 Ct. Cases No. 8521/2019 Kailash Chand vs. Deevansh Bhatia Page No. 12 of 15 25. The ld. counsel for the complainant had confronted the accused with Ex. DW1/C1 and Ex. DW1/C2, without revealing the title of the document and had asked the accused to identify his signatures therein. The accused, after perusing the signatures therein, had stated that the signatures on the said documents were not his. It was later revealed that the said documents were the accused's own application seeking permission to inspect the file and seeking permission to cross-examine the complainant u/s 145 (2) NI Act. Relying on this blatant denial of the accused regarding his own signatures on his own application, the ld. counsel for the complainant has argued that the accused has lost his credibility as a witness and is wrongly denying his signatures on the Promissory Note. Considering the hitherto wrongful denials of the accused regarding his address, the misleading answers regarding the make and model of the mobile phone and now regarding his signatures on his own application, the court finds that the accused has lost his credibility as a witness on three counts till now. In the light of this, his denial on the Promissory Note would not fetch any favourable outcome to him. 26. When the accused has himself lost his credibility, the complainant cannot be asked to take more and more evidentiary burden and to call an expert witness at his instance, to engage with the platitudinous denial of the accused regarding his signature on the Promissory Note. If the version of the accused is to be believed also, it has not come forth that the accused has taken any prudent steps by filing any police complaint against the alleged misuse of his cheque in question and regarding the alleged forgery of his signatures on the Promissory Note. Accordingly, the argument of the ld. counsel for the accused that the complainant has not been able to produce any proof of the alleged loan in question, is rejected. (C) That the friendly loan without any consideration cannot be called a Digitally signed legally enforceable liability: TANMAY by TANMAY BATHAM BATHAM Date: 2026.07.30 15:31:27 +0530 Ct. Cases No. 8521/2019 Kailash Chand vs. Deevansh Bhatia Page No. 13 of 15 27. The ld. counsel for the accused has argued that as per the judgment of Hon'ble Hight Court of Jharkhand in Md. Masudul Haque Ansari @ M. H. Ansari vs. The State of Jharkhand (Acquittal Appeal No. 10 of 2012), a friendly loan without any commercial consideration cannot be called a Contract as per the Indian Contract Act, 1872 and as such the transaction cannot be legally enforced u/s 138 of the NI Act. 28. The above-said argument of the ld. counsel for the accused is being dismissed at the threshold. The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in the landmark judgment of Sanjabij Tari vs Kishore S.Borcar [Criminal Appeal No. 1755 of 2010] has affirmed a case of conviction in a case which was arising out of the friendly loan transaction. The Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in Amit Jain vs Sanjeev Kumar Singh & Anr. (CRL.A. 1248/2019) has even gone ahead to hold that in cases of friendly loans, proof by way of documentary evidence should not be insisted always, thereby affirming the enforceability of friendly loan in cases arising out of Section 138 of the NI Act. Hence, in the light of the above said judgments, it can be said that the transactions arising out of friendly loans can be validly enforced in the cases pertaining to Section 138 of the NI Act. Accordingly, the argument of the ld. counsel for the accused is rejected. (D) That the bank account of the accused was lying dormant since years: 29. The accused, in his DE, has brought on record his bank account statement for the period to 09.11.2015 to 26.11.2019 (Ex. DW1/1). The ld. counsel for the accused has argued that the said statement shows that the bank account of the accused has been dormant after 30.03.2016 and it is unlikely that the accused will issue cheque from such an account. The perusal of the bank statement of the accused shows that it has indeed remained dormant from the said date. However, it also reflects that in a transaction dated 07.09.2019 the accused was charged for the dishonour of the cheque in question on 27.08.2019. Digitally signed by TANMAY TANMAY BATHAM BATHAM Date: 2026.07.30 15:31:33 +0530 Ct. Cases No. 8521/2019 Kailash Chand vs. Deevansh Bhatia Page No. 14 of 15 The bank account statement (Ex. DW1/1) only proves that the said bank account of the accused has been dormant, and not "closed" or "blocked" etc. Notably, even the cheque in question has also been dishonoured due to the insufficiency of funds in bank account of the accused and not due to the dormancy of the bank account. Hence, the bank account statement of the accused is not found to be addressing the merits of the present case. Accordingly, the argument of the ld. counsel for the accused that it is unlikely that the accused will issue cheque from a dormant bank account, is rejected. 30. Therefore, in view of the discussion in the foregoing paragraphs, the inevitable conclusion is that the accused has failed to prove that there was no legally enforceable liability of the amount mentioned in the cheque in question. Therefore, the second ingredient is also proved in the present case. CONCLUSION 31. To recapitulate the above discussion, the signature on the cheque in question is admitted by the accused and the presumption under Section 118 and Section 139 of NI Act is raised against the accused. The accused has failed to rebut the said presumption by raising a probable defence. Resultantly, the complaint of the complainant Mr. Kailash Chand is allowed and the accused Mr. Deevansh Bhatia is hereby convicted of the offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. 32. Let the convict be heard separately on quantum of sentence. A copy of this judgment containing 15 pages be given free of cost to the convict.
